The theoretical section, while limited, provides a reasonable conceptual link between routing structure, effective dimension, and generalization.
weaknesses: The central claims are stronger than the evidence. The study appears to rely on a single MoE model family and one pretraining trajectory, so it is unclear whether the observed behavior is a general LLM pretraining phenomenon or an OLMoE-specific artifact.

The definition of local grokking is partly post hoc: benchmark samples are grouped by when predictions become consistently correct, and correlations are computed after accuracy begins its sustained rise. This weakens the claim that the proposed metrics predict or monitor generalization prospectively.

The empirical analysis uses only 10 checkpoints, giving very few points for the reported high correlations and p-values. There are no confidence intervals, robustness tests, held-out domains, or statistical controls for checkpoint/time trends.

Instruction tuning is a serious confound. Each checkpoint is LoRA-tuned before evaluation, but the extent to which changes in downstream performance reflect pretraining versus SFT dynamics is not convincingly isolated.

Important implementation details are underspecified, including the memorization thresholds epsilon/delta, routing-weight thresholds for pathway extraction, exact benchmark scoring protocols, and sensitivity of results to these choices.

The proposed metrics are described as zero-cost, but computing routing pathways and pairwise edit distances over training samples requires access to data, router activations, and nontrivial compute; the practical monitoring cost is understated.

There is an inconsistency around the pathway consistency metric: the formula seems to define lower values as smoother/more consistent, while the text and correlation table describe consistency as increasing with generalization.

The theory is quite far from the empirical setting: it assumes fixed routing and an NTK regime for a simplified MoE, whereas the paper studies deep pretrained MoEs with learned evolving routers. The theorem is essentially a standard kernel ridge-style bound and does not tightly justify the specific proposed metrics.

The paper would be much stronger with ablations against random or shuffled routes, alternative similarity metrics, additional MoE checkpoints/models, dense-model comparisons or adaptations, and a true prospective prediction experiment.

weaknesses: The central claim that the paper verifies grokking in LLM pretraining is not convincingly established. The definition of memorization is based on low or converged next-token loss on pretraining samples, which can also reflect interpolation or general language modeling ability, especially in a one-epoch setting where some samples may not have been directly learned by replay.

The empirical evidence is too narrow for the breadth of the claims: essentially one 7B MoE model, about 10 checkpoints, no seeds, no other architectures, no dense-model comparison, and no replication across model scales or pretraining runs.

The downstream generalization protocol is heavily confounded by LoRA instruction tuning separately applied to checkpoints. Accuracy changes may reflect checkpoint-specific finetuning behavior, adapter optimization, prompts, or SFT data interactions rather than pretraining generalization itself.

The correlation analysis is weak evidence for monitoring ability. Correlations appear to be computed over very few checkpoints and after selecting the phase where accuracy already rises, so high Pearson/Spearman values may mostly reflect shared monotonic trends. There is no prospective prediction, held-out-domain validation, uncertainty analysis, or robust baseline such as checkpoint index/time.

Several analysis choices seem post hoc or under-specified, including memorization thresholds, pathway expert-selection thresholds, grouping by memorization time, choosing only samples that eventually become correct, and matching train/test groups with SentenceTransformer plus Hungarian matching. These choices could manufacture the appearance of local grokking.

The proposed metrics are conceptually and mathematically shaky. Edit distance over stringified expert IDs is sensitive to arbitrary formatting and routing-threshold choices, and the pathway consistency definition/sign appears inconsistent with the paper's narrative and reported positive correlations.

The theoretical section is generic and only loosely connected to the empirical claims. It analyzes a simplified fixed-router NTK/ridge setting and a synthetic one-layer MoE, while the main phenomenon concerns evolving routers in a deep pretrained MoE; it does not substantively prove that the measured routing metrics cause or explain grokking.

The claimed 'zero-cost' monitoring tool is overstated: it requires access to training data, internal routing weights, MoE architecture, and forward passes through a large model, and its usefulness is demonstrated only retrospectively after expensive benchmark evaluation.

Reproducibility and clarity are limited: key hyperparameters, thresholds, exact checkpoint identities, prompts, evaluation metrics, statistical tests, p-values, and code availability are insufficiently specified, and several figures/tables are difficult to interpret.

The pathway consistency metric is confusingly defined: the formula appears to make lower values correspond to smoother routing, while the text and correlation table interpret higher values as better consistency/generalization.

The theory assumes fixed routing and NTK-style expert training, which is far from the claimed phenomenon of evolving routing pathways during LLM pretraining; it supports intuition but not the main causal claim.

The metrics are presented as near-zero-cost, but computing routing pathways over training samples and checkpoints for a 7B MoE is still nontrivial; the cost comparison against validation evaluation or lightweight probes is not quantified.
Reproducibility is incomplete: exact checkpoint IDs, prompts, evaluation protocol, seeds, domain-specific epsilon values, and code availability are not specified in enough detail.
Data contamination handling via removing the top 10% Min-K%++ scores is heuristic and not validated, which matters for benchmarks such as MMLU, HumanEval-style tasks, and web-derived corpora.

strengths: The topic is interesting: understanding delayed generalization and internal routing dynamics during LLM pretraining would be valuable if demonstrated convincingly.
The paper attempts to use public OLMoE checkpoints and proposes concrete MoE routing-path metrics, which are at least inspectable in principle.
The appendix includes several robustness-style analyses, including threshold variation, LoRA rank variation, routing entropy, cross-domain comparisons, and a small nanoMoE replication.
weaknesses: The central claim that the paper observes grokking in LLM pretraining is not well supported. The definition of memorization as low/stable token loss and generalization as downstream benchmark accuracy after separate LoRA finetuning is far removed from the standard grokking setup, and the paper does not convincingly justify that this is the same phenomenon rather than ordinary checkpoint-dependent capability growth.

The evaluation appears heavily post hoc and selection-biased. The paper focuses on samples that eventually become consistently correct and analyzes checkpoints after accuracy begins a sustained rise, which can manufacture strong correlations with any metric that changes monotonically with training time.

The proposed pathway metrics are not shown to predict generalization out of sample. Correlations are computed on very few checkpoints, without confidence intervals, exact p-values, multiple-comparison handling, or strong baselines such as checkpoint index, random monotone trends, expert load, activation similarity, or representation probes.

Instruction tuning is a major confound. Each checkpoint is LoRA-tuned before evaluation, with task-specific SFT datasets, so downstream performance may reflect finetuning dynamics, prompt-following ability, or SFT/test contamination rather than pretrained generalization. This also weakens the claimed “evaluation-free” monitoring contribution.

The training-test pairing via SentenceTransformer similarity and Hungarian matching is arbitrary and does not establish a causal or mechanistic link between memorized pretraining groups and benchmark samples. Group sizes, thresholds, and stability criteria are insufficiently reported.

There are serious dataset inconsistencies. The paper claims 10,000 test examples per domain, but benchmarks such as HumanEvalPlus and MMLU college_chemistry do not have that scale. This raises substantial concerns about experimental validity and reproducibility.

The pathway metric definitions are technically questionable. Edit distance over comma-separated expert-index strings may be sensitive to tokenization and delimiters rather than routing structure, and the pathway consistency formula appears semantically inconsistent with the text. Comparing router weight rows across different layers as embeddings is also not well justified.

The theory is largely disconnected from the experiments. It analyzes a fixed-router, one-layer/NTK-style MoE ridge-regression setting, while the empirical claims concern full transformer MoE pretraining with changing routers and autoregressive language modeling. The claimed link from edit distance to effective dimension is only supported by a small synthetic experiment, not by OLMoE evidence.

The paper lacks convincing controls or interventions. It does not show that changing routing pathways changes generalization, nor that the metrics work prospectively on held-out domains, models, seeds, or independently trained runs.

Presentation and reproducibility are weak: important implementation details are missing, several claims are overstated, figure/table evidence is visually compressed, the p-value legend is unclear, and there are textual/formatting issues such as an apparent missing nanoMoE footnote.

strengths: The paper studies an important and underexplored question: whether memorization-to-generalization dynamics resembling grokking appear during realistic LLM pretraining rather than only in small synthetic settings.
The proposed routing-pathway view for MoE models is interesting and potentially useful; pathway distance and cross-layer routing consistency are intuitive diagnostics for internal reorganization.

The empirical study covers multiple downstream domains and includes several useful robustness checks, including routing-threshold sensitivity, LoRA-rank sensitivity, cross-domain pathway distances, routing entropy, and a smaller nanoMoE replication.
The manuscript is generally well organized and connects empirical observations with a theoretical lens based on routing kernels and effective dimension.
weaknesses: The central claim that this is grokking in LLM pretraining is not fully established. The definition of memorization is retrospective and threshold-based, and delayed downstream improvement could be explained by continued learning from later related data, checkpoint time, LoRA tuning effects, or general capability growth rather than a grokking-like transition.

The evidence for pathway metrics as generalization monitors is weakened by very small sample size: correlations are computed over only a handful of checkpoints, often after selecting the post-rise regime. Monotonic time trends could produce high correlations, and stronger baselines such as checkpoint index, cumulative tokens, random monotone metrics, router entropy per domain, and simple training-progress features are missing.

There is a serious inconsistency in the pathway consistency definition and interpretation. The formula defines lower values as smoother/more consistent, but figures and tables treat increasing values as improved consistency and positively correlated with accuracy. This ambiguity directly affects one of the two main metrics.

The training-test pairing procedure via SentenceTransformer embeddings and Hungarian matching is heuristic and does not support causal claims that memorizing a training group drives a specific downstream group’s generalization. Some plotted delayed jumps are partly induced by defining test groups according to when they become correct.

The evaluation is not sufficiently reproducible or statistically convincing: important details such as exact prompts, decoding settings, checkpoint-wise accuracy values, group sizes, variance across LoRA seeds, and confidence intervals are missing. The p-value/color presentation is hard to audit with so few checkpoints.

The theoretical analysis is only loosely connected to the empirical phenomenon. It assumes fixed routing and NTK-style expert training, whereas the main claims concern evolving multi-layer MoE routing during pretraining. The edit-distance-to-effective-dimension link is empirical on a toy setup rather than a derived guarantee.

The scope is narrower than the claims suggest: the main evidence is from one 7B MoE model, with a much smaller nanoMoE follow-up. The paper does not show that the conclusions hold for other large MoEs, dense LLMs, different pretraining mixtures, or multiple training seeds.

Some claims are overstated, especially that the metrics have near-zero cost and are finetuning/evaluation-free. Computing routing pathways over many samples and checkpoints still requires nontrivial forward passes, and the claimed usefulness is validated only by downstream evaluations and LoRA-tuned checkpoints.
